Last week, I posted a PMP scenario:

A sponsor wants to skip a planned stakeholder review to hit a date. The team can meet the date, but a high-impact dependency may be affected. What do you do first?

Three people answered. All three chose the same thing — assess the dependency impact with the relevant stakeholders — and all three were right.

Bryan Koh gave the reason rather than just the letter: the question asks what you do FIRST. You ASSESS, before you act.

Here's the part worth noting:

"Assess first" is correct here, but it isn't a rule. It's a response to one word in the stem: "may." A high-impact dependency MAY be affected. That's unresolved uncertainty, and you can't accept it, escalate it, or document your way out of not knowing.

Change that one word and the answer changes with it.

If the stem said the dependency WILL slip go-live by three weeks, the uncertainty is already resolved. Assessing again is stalling. Now the real choice is between escalating and replanning — and "assess" becomes the wrong answer.

That's what the updated exam is actually testing: act at the level of information the scenario gives you.

Candidates who memorize "always assess first" pass the easy version of this question and miss the hard one, because the hard version already did the assessing for them.

The tell is in the verb. "May be affected" means go find out. "Will be affected" means ... decide.

C. Assess the dependency impact with the relevant stakeholders.

A vendor misses a contracted milestone. Your schedule carries two weeks of float. The vendor says they will recover it.

A. Use the float and monitor
B. Follow the remedy the contract defines for a missed milestone
C. Escalate to procurement
D. Re-baseline the schedule

The tell is "contracted". Once a stem names the agreement, the agreement governs.

When you hire a security analyst, what you are actually buying is their judgment under partial information.

The tooling is commodity now. Everyone has the same EDR and it fires for everyone. The separation shows up in the first few minutes after it fires, when the analyst has an incomplete picture, a live business on the other side of the call, and nobody free to ask.

Here is a Security+ scenario that lives in those few minutes.

Your EDR fires at 10:40 on a Tuesday. A finance workstation is authenticating to three servers it has never touched, using credentials that belong to someone in another department.

Two hundred people are working. Nobody has reported anything.

What do you do first?

A. Pull the full telemetry and authentication logs to rule out a false positive
B. Isolate the workstation from the network
C. Notify the incident response lead and wait for direction
D. Disable the account and force a password reset

The incident response lifecycle puts analysis before containment, which is exactly what makes this hard. Three of these are defensible on a quiet afternoon. One of them is right while something is still moving.

Post your letter and, more importantly, your reason.

Full elimination on all four options goes in this thread tonight, comments or no comments.

As promised — the full elimination on all four.

B. Isolate the workstation.

A — pull the telemetry first. Analysis before containment is the textbook lifecycle, and that is exactly why this item is hard. But the lifecycle assumes you have time to spend. Credentials from another department authenticating to three servers they have never touched is not ambiguous enough to spend it. You investigate a contained host, not a live one.

C — notify the IR lead and wait. Right escalation, wrong sequencing. Notification is not containment. While you wait for direction, the session keeps authenticating.

D — disable the account and force a reset. The closest wrong answer, and the one most people pick. It addresses the credentials and not the host. If the workstation is compromised the attacker still holds it, and you have just told them you noticed.

B contains the blast radius while preserving the evidence. Isolation keeps memory and disk state intact; a reset does not.

The tell most people read past: "Two hundred people are working." That is not colour. That is the scope of what you are protecting while you decide.

The point of a working agreement is not the rule. It is that everyone on the team can predict everyone else without having to ask.

Which means an agreement is worth exactly what the team believes about it on the day it gets tested.

Here is one of those days.

Your team’s working agreement says no merges after Thursday noon without a second reviewer.

A team member merged a hotfix alone on Friday night. It worked. A customer outage was resolved before Monday. Two other engineers have since asked whether the rule still applies.

What do you do?

A. Thank her publicly for the save and treat the agreement as guidance rather than a gate.
B. Address the violation with her privately, reaffirm the ground rule with the team, then have the team decide whether it needs a documented emergency path.
C. Add an emergency-outage exception to the working agreement.
D. Escalate the breach to her functional manager as a discipline matter.

The outcome was good. That is what makes it hard.

One letter, then your reason. I read the reasons.

C is the one I expected to take people, and it is the interesting wrong answer. The team probably does need a documented emergency path. Writing it is tidy, it is forward-looking, and it closes the exact gap the incident exposed.

It is still the wrong first move. Amending the agreement before you address the breach teaches the team that breaking a rule is how you get the rule changed. The two engineers asking whether it still applies are running that test right now.

B rectifies the violation, reaffirms the agreement, and then lets the team decide whether it needs changing. Same emergency path, opposite order, completely different lesson.

The pattern: rectify the violation first. A good outcome does not ratify a breach.

What do you do?

B. Record it in the lessons-learned log for the program's end-of-project closure report.
C. Require the vendor to revise their own procedure, and hold them to it contractually.
D. Change your team's handover step this week and keep the integration schedule moving.

D is the one that looks like follow-through. It is the fastest route to the outcome you are actually accountable for, and it needs no meeting outside your own team.

D reaches for money when the thing you have actually lost is the integration test window. Contingency does not buy a test window back.

B does three separate things, and the sequence matters: reclassify it (risk to issue), execute the response you already planned, then reassess what it did downstream.

Risk management does not end when a risk occurs. That is when it changes register.

A is the answer I expect to take people, and it is the one that shows why a letter without a reason is worth nothing. Keeping the register current is diligent, the tool asks you for it, and it is what a healthy risk process looks like from outside the project.

It is still a category error. The thing has happened. There is no probability left to revise, and re-scoring it keeps an issue filed under the wrong instrument while the downstream work goes unassessed.

C escalates for an extension before anyone knows the downstream impact, which treats the symptom ahead of the intervention. D may well be the right funding source, but drawing the reserve is a funding action, not management of the impediment.

B switches instruments: issue log, apply the response as an intervention, reassess what it does to the work downstream.

The pattern: detect the state change from risk to issue, then switch instruments. A number you can still update is not evidence that the number still means anything.

posts.copy:
I asked ChatGPT for ten intermediate PMP questions. Then I put one of them next to one of mine.

Theirs:

A previously identified risk occurs and begins affecting the schedule. A planned contingency response exists. What should the project manager do next?

A. Implement the planned risk response
B. Immediately escalate the risk to the sponsor
C. Create a new risk management plan
D. Remove the risk from the risk register

Mine:

A risk you identified carried a $180,000 contingency allocation. It just materialized at $210,000. You hold no unallocated budget, and the $30,000 difference pushes you past your approved cost baseline.

A. Draw the full $210,000 from contingency reserve and report the overrun in the next status report
B. Apply the $180,000 contingency, and request the $30,000 through the governance process that controls management reserve and baseline change
C. Absorb the $30,000 by deferring a discretionary scope item to a later release
D. Re-estimate the remaining work to find $30,000 of savings before reporting anything

Both are about a risk that materialized when a response was already planned.

The first has one defensible option and three nobody would pick. The second has four things a working PM has actually done on a real Tuesday.

I am not going to tell you the first question is bad. It is a reasonable warm-up and it took eleven seconds to produce. If you are three months out, it is fine.

But the exam does not test whether you know a contingency plan should be used. It tests whether you know which pot the money comes from when the number goes over — and whether you know that crossing a cost baseline was never your call to make.

That distinction is the difference between passing and being surprised.

Which one would you rather be practicing the night before?

Give me the letter you would pick on the second one, and your reason. The reason is the part I read.

Answer and full breakdown in the first comment.

CipherExam works every PMP question this way — the reasoning, not the letter. Free 7 days, no card.

Finance planning sits in Process, which is 41% of the exam.

#PMP #ProjectManagement
posts.firstComment:
As promised — the answer and the full breakdown.

B. Apply the $180,000 contingency, then request the $30,000 through the governance process that controls management reserve and baseline change.

A is what almost everybody actually does, and it answers a different question. Contingency covers identified risks up to what was allocated. Drawing $210,000 against a $180,000 allocation and noting it in a status report is a baseline change performed by press release.

C trades scope for cost without the change control that governs either. D is the most respectable-looking wrong answer: re-estimating to find savings before reporting means the sponsor learns about the overrun after you have decided what to do about it.

The split in B is the whole point. The $180,000 is yours — allocated for exactly this. The $30,000 is not, because it crosses the cost baseline, and crossing a baseline is never a PM's call.

The numbers were never the hard part. Which pot the money comes from is.

And that is the gap between the two questions above. Not that one came from a model. That one was written to a standard and kept, and the other was the first thing out.
